title: 银行里的夜间保洁：桑娅·伊韦科维奇为不可见女性所做的试镜

zh: 银行里的夜间保洁：桑娅·伊韦科维奇为不可见女性所做的试镜
en: Night cleaning at the bank: Sanja Iveković’s screen tests for invisible women

zh: 克拉拉·肯普-韦尔奇
en: KLARA KEMP-WELCH

zh: 2016年，埃斯特集团银行股份公司（Erste Group Bank AG）在维也纳贝尔维德区开设了新总部——埃斯特园区（Erste Campus），由亨克·施赖克建筑事务所设计。首席执行官安德烈亚斯·特赖希尔（曾被《欧洲货币》评为2019年“年度银行家”）解释说，他想废除传统办公空间，把所有人迁入一栋建筑，使一切变得非常“开放”。埃斯特园区将成为一个“让人感觉良好”的空间，一个用于“团队建设”的空间，在那里，“员工、客户以及所有希望与我们共同塑造未来的人可以聚在一起”，从而产生一个“鼓舞人心且令人兴奋的工作场所，促进个人与团队之间的交流，增强团队凝聚力”。银行网站把该园区描述为“银行业的新型工作环境”：一种“新企业文化的办公理念”。
这段简介的乐观语调，与贝尔维德区本身的整体愿景一致。正如埃斯特集团网站所解释的：
en: In 2016, Erste Group Bank AG opened a new headquarters – Erste Campus – in the Quartier Belvedere District in Vienna, designed by Henke Schreieck architects. CEO Andreas Treichl (named Euromoney’s ‘Banker of the Year’ 2019) has explained that he had wanted to do away with conventional office spaces and to move everyone into a single building to make everything very ‘open’. Erste Campus was to be a space ‘to feel good about’; a space for ‘team building’ where ‘staff, customers and everyone who wishes to shape the future with us can come together’ to produce an ‘inspiring and exhilarating workplace, promoting communication between individuals and teams and strengthening team cohesion’. The bank’s website describes the Campus as ‘a new working environment for banking’: an ‘office concept of new corporate culture’.
The upbeat tone of this blurb is in line with the wider vision for the Quartier Belvedere itself. As the Erste Group site explains:

zh: 该街区的投资者将提供一种此地从未有过的工作与生活方式：入驻该街区的公司员工在工作日结束时不会立刻回家，而是与同事、居民以及旅人一起留在贝尔维德区，为一天画上积极的句号。
en: investors in this district will be providing a way of living and  working here never experienced before: workers in the firms establishing themselves in this district will not immediately head for  home at the end of the working day, but will stay on in the Quartier  Belvedere together with their colleagues, with residents and with  travellers and bring the day to a positive close.

zh: 于是，新街区与埃斯特园区都倡导一种新的企业工作场所模式；这症候性地体现了营造新型工作环境、以支持更大“灵活性”、提高员工投入、生产率与利润的驱动力；这是欧洲银行业学习圣克拉拉谷歌总部（Googleplex）成功经验的一次实验。
en: Both the new district and Erste Campus, then, champion a new approach to the corporate workplace, symptomatic of the drive to deliver new working environments supporting greater ‘flexibility’, increasing worker commitment, productivity and profits; a Euro-banking experiment in learning from the successes of Googleplex, Santa Clara.

zh: 埃斯特园区处处坚持使用玻璃，症候性地体现了企业建筑在观念上对透明性的依附。在采访中，米夏埃尔·维尔纳（埃斯特集团银行股份公司房地产投资与运营主管）把透明描述为“我们的核心价值之一：当你审视流程时，你知道发生了什么”。他解释说：
en: The insistence on glass throughout the Erste Campus is symptomatic of corporate architecture’s conceptual attachment to transparency. In interview, Michael Werner (head of Real Estate Investment and Operations, Erste Group AG) describes transparency as ‘one of our core values: when you look into the process, you know what happens’. He explains:

zh: 透明性的承诺也应当由办公大楼来例示；因此，你能够从外部看到内部，这一点很重要。我们不向客户隐藏；处理资金的金融服务提供者似乎总是在秘密或地下的地方做些什么，没人能进入。而在这里，你可以直接看到建筑内部。
en: the promise of transparency should also be exemplified by the  office building; so it’s important that you can look into the interior  from the outside. We don’t hide from the client; financial services  providers handling money always seem to be doing something in  secret or underground, where nobody has access. Here you can look  directly into the building.

zh: 然而，这样的工作环境也带来挑战：
en: Nevertheless, such a working environment brings challenges:

zh: 透明不是一个轻松的话题；对人来说有时非常困难。在开放空间里、桌面整洁地工作，意味着完全透明……我们需要特定的工作环境，才能真正高效或富有创造力。
en: Transparency is not an easy topic; sometimes it is very difficult  for people. Working in an open space with a clean desk means full  transparency … we need a specific working environment in order to  be really efficient or creative.

zh: 当被问及为何觉得有必要为该项目制作一本“氛围手册”时，维尔纳解释说：
en: Asked about why he had felt the need to produce a ‘mood book’ for the project, Werner explains:

zh: 开发企业总部的过程并不意味着把公司的企业身份转译为物理空间。相反，它是要理解品牌态度，并将其转化为一种品牌氛围。理想情况下，品牌不应对园区使用者或访客过于可见——相反，他们应当感受到它。
en: The process of developing corporate headquarters does not imply  translating the corporate identity of the company into physical  space. Instead, it is to understand the brand attitude and to transform it into a brand atmosphere. Ideally, the brand should not  be too visible to the user or a visitor to the Campus – instead, they  should feel it.

zh: 他接着说：
en: He goes on:

zh: 我们想传达埃斯特如何看待某些问题、我们如何看待事物、我们希望客户如何看待我们和我们的工作。这与我们的顾问工作有关，与我们如何对待客户和员工有关，也与我们在日常业务中希望如何行事有关。
en: we wanted to convey how Erste thinks about certain issues, how  we see things, how we want clients to see us and our work. This is  related to our advisor work and how we treat both customers and  employees, and how we want to conduct ourselves in daily business.

zh: 埃斯特集团是“中欧和东欧最大的金融服务提供者之一”，
拥有47,000名员工，核心市场在奥地利、克罗地亚、捷克共和国、匈牙利、罗马尼亚、塞尔维亚和斯洛伐克，次级市场在波斯尼亚、摩尔多瓦、黑山、北马其顿和斯洛文尼亚。
公司创新中心（Erste HUB）负责人鲍里斯·马特强调了这一历史地点对于总部选址的特殊意义：
en: The Erste Group is ‘among the largest financial service providers in Central and Eastern Europe’,

with 47,000 employees, and core markets in Austria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Serbia and Slovakia, as well as secondary markets in Bosnia, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Slovenia.
Boris Marte, head of the company’s Innovation Centre (Erste HUB) stresses the particular relevance of the historic site for the location of the headquarters:

zh: 我们把场地建在“南站”（Südbahnhof）旧址上，那是这座城市南面的火车站……1960和70年代，数十万来自共产主义东欧的人抵达这座车站，寻找某种类似自由的东西……1970年代，数十万来自苏联的犹太人也来到这里，然后继续前往以色列……南站曾在铁幕仍然存在的时代作为重要枢纽拥有自己的历史。这是人们来往于东方与东南方之间的唯一火车站。在这样一个地方建设一家在这些国家有着强大存在的公司，承载着某种信息。
en: We constructed our venue on the former site of the ‘Südbahnhof’,  the city’s southern railway station… In the 1960s and 70s, hundreds  of thousands of people from communist Eastern Europe arrived at  this train station to look for something like freedom … in the 1970s,  hundreds of thousands of Jews from the Soviet Union also arrived  here and then travelled on to Israel … the Südbahnhof had its history  as an important hub at a time when the iron curtain still existed.  This was the only train station where people moved back and forth  between the East and the Southeast. Building a company that is  strongly represented in those countries in that very place carries a  certain message.

zh: 这一“信息”想必意在提醒人们维也纳曾是其前社会主义邻国的中转站；但这座庞大建筑的拆除以及新商业区的建设，也标志着优先事项的重大转变。如果这一地点曾经编排着人员跨越国境的流动，那么如今它主要被设计为资本流动的枢纽。
en: The ‘message’ is presumably intended to be a reminder of Vienna’s role as a way station for its former socialist neighbours, but the demolition of the massive structure and the construction of the new business district also mark a significant shift in priorities. If the site once orchestrated the flow of people across borders, it is now primarily designed in as a hub for the flow of capital.

zh: 银行对前东方阵营“回馈”的承诺，更清楚地体现在其慈善分支埃斯特基金会（ERSTE Foundation）上；在乔治·索罗斯从1990年代的当代艺术中心网络中撤资后，该地区新兴当代艺术界留下资金缺口，而基金会一直是填补这一缺口的主要力量。基金会致力于三个核心领域：“社会创新、欧洲凝聚与民主、当代文化”，并参与了广泛的文化计划：创立康塔克特收藏（Kontakt Collection）——埃斯特集团与埃斯特基金会的艺术收藏——专门收藏该地区的现代与当代艺术；资助 Tranzit——一个“在奥地利、罗马尼亚、斯洛伐克、捷克共和国和匈牙利开展当代艺术自主计划的网络”；并赞助伊戈尔·扎贝尔文化与理论奖等。
基金会还发布在线访谈与故事，主题包括罗姆儿童教育及斯洛伐克学校的隔离、克罗地亚的制药污染、波斯尼亚未能安置流离失所者、波兰与欧盟的冲突路线、波斯尼亚—克罗地亚边境营地中难民的困境、科索沃的青年，以及保加利亚维丁的凋敝——那里被称为“世界人口衰退之都”。
因此，基金会致力于介入与后社会主义语境相关的一系列广泛人权与平等问题。
en: The bank’s commitment to ‘giving back’ to the former East is better evidenced by its philanthropic wing, the ERSTE Foundation, which has been the main plug for the funding gap left in the region’s emerging contemporary art world after George Soros pulled his money out of the 1990s’ network of Centres for Contemporary Art. The Foundation is devoted to three core areas: ‘social innovation, European cohesion and democracy and contemporary culture’ and has engaged in a wide range of cultural initiatives: the founding of the Kontakt Collection – the Erste Group and ERSTE Foundation art collection – dedicated to modern and contemporary art from the region; the funding of the Tranzit – a ‘network of autonomous initiatives in contemporary art in Austria, Romania, Slovakia, Czech Republic and Hungary’; and the sponsoring of the Igor Zabel Award for Culture and Theory, among others.

The Foundation also publishes online interviews and stories on topics such as the education of Roma children and segregation in Slovak schools, pharma pollution in Croatia, Bosnia’s failure to house its displaced, Poland’s collision course with the EU, the plight of refugees in camps on the Bosnian–Croatian border, the youth of Kosovo, and the emptying of Bulgaria’s Vidin, ‘the world capital of population decline’.
The Foundation, then, is committed to engaging with a wide range of human rights and equality issues relevant to the post-socialist context.

zh: 当埃斯特集团开始考虑如何在园区中运用艺术时，他们很想避免把艺术当作一种通用的企业室内设计形式（大幅面、抽象绘画、全球摄影）。园区《氛围手册》明确指出：“没有法律规定企业总部的墙上必须装饰艺术。我们只在认为艺术具有相关性、并且能够为埃斯特园区的所有使用者和访客带来灵感的地方展示艺术。”在为新园区委托创作艺术品时，集团选择了中欧和东欧艺术家的新作，这些作品“要求艺术家不仅考虑埃斯特集团运营所在的地缘政治区域语境，还要在项目中参照埃斯特园区建筑的特征及其位于南站旧址的位置”。
该项目后来被称为“建筑中的艺术”，是与康塔克特收藏负责人卡特琳·罗姆贝格的合作。策展人兼联合委托方皮埃尔·巴尔-布朗解释说，该项目旨在“重新思考艺术与资本的关系，并考察当使用者、银行家和雇主这些在这家金融企业场所交汇的视角彼此趋同或相互矛盾时，被强加的妥协”。他还说：“任何在私人土地上发展的计划都有其盲点，一种被压抑的意识，一旦展览结束便显露出来……暴露出使这家银行重新焕发活力的矛盾的生机。”
en: When Erste Group came to consider how they would deploy art as part of the Campus, they were keen to avoid using it as a generic form of corporate interior design (large format, abstract painting, global photography). The Campus ‘Mood Book’ explicitly makes the point that ‘there is no law stating that the walls of corporate headquarters have to be adorned with art. We only display art where we believe it has relevance and can be an inspiration for all Erste Campus users and visitors.’ In commissioning artwork for its new campus, the Group opted for new work by artists from central and eastern Europe which ‘required the artists not only to take into account the context of the geopolitical area in which Erste Group operates, but also to make reference in the projects to the character and location of the Erste Campus building on the former site of the Südbahnhof railway station’.

‘Art in Architecture’, as the project came to be called, was a collaboration with Kathrin Rhomberg, head of the Kontakt collection. The curator and co-commissioner, Pierre Bal-Blanc, explained that the project was about ‘rethinking the relationship between art and capital, and examining the compromises imposed when the viewpoints of users, bankers and employers who cross paths at the site of this financial enterprise converge or contradict one another’. He added that ‘Any initiative developed on private terrain has its blind spot, a repressed consciousness that reveals itself once the exhibit is finished … exposing the vitality of contradictions that revitalize this bank.’

zh: 本文对园区及其抱负的简短介绍所引用的许多埃斯特代表陈述，是由克罗地亚艺术家桑娅·伊韦科维奇收集的，作为她为影片《埃斯特园区里不可见的女性》进行的“田野调查”的一部分；该片由她编剧和导演，并作为“建筑中的艺术”委托项目的一部分在园区内展出。埃斯特园区建筑面积广阔，达165,000平方米。当伊韦科维奇问马特，他认为园区里有多少清洁工时，他回答说：“我猜在100到150之间。”伊韦科维奇温和地反驳：“我也是这么想的，但实际只有58人。”她解释说：“作为女性主义者，我感兴趣的是女性在这里工作的处境和条件。当我受邀做一个项目，看到这座巨大的建筑时，我脑中浮现的第一个问题是：谁在清洁这一切？因此，我的项目是关于清洁女工的。”
关于埃斯特代表希望通过园区设计传达的“感受”之性质，伊韦科维奇指出：“你们强调想看到每个人，也让人人可见，能够与每个人交谈并沟通。我正在做的项目——讨论交流以及在这里受雇的每个人——追求的是同一个目标。”
《埃斯特园区里不可见的女性》试图检验该集团对“透明”的企业承诺，其方式确保清洁这栋建筑的女性被楼里的每个人看见。这部与清洁女工合作完成的影片，是对她们不可见劳动的一首颂歌。影片在A—F座0—9层电梯厅的一系列显示器上播放。
en: Many of the statements by Erste representatives cited in this brief introduction to the Campus and its ambitions were gathered by Croatian artist Sanja Iveković as part of her ‘field research’ for a film piece entitled

, which she wrote and directed, and installed on Campus as part of the ‘Art in Architecture’ commission. The floor area of Erste Campus is vast, standing at 165,000 m2. When Iveković asked Marte how many cleaners he thought there are on Campus, he replied: ‘I guess between 100 and 150’. Iveković countered gently: ‘That’s what I thought, too, but there are only 58.’ She explained: ‘As a feminist I’m interested in the situation and the conditions under which women are working here. When I was invited to do a project and saw the big building, the first question that came to my mind was, who’s cleaning all this? Thus, my project is about the cleaning ladies.’

With reference to the nature of the ‘feeling’ Erste representatives wanted to convey through the Campus design, Iveković noted: ‘you stressed you wanted to see everybody and also everybody to be seen, to be able to talk to everyone and communicate with them. The project I’m working on – talking about communication and everybody who is employed here – is pursuing the same goal.’

children: The Invisible Women of the Erste Campus

en: set out to test the Group’s corporate commitment to ‘transparency’ by making sure that the women who clean the building were made visible to everyone in the building. The film, made collaboratively with the cleaners, is an ode to their invisible labour. It is played on a series of monitors in the Elevator areas of Levels 0–9 in Building A–F.

zh: 影片在黑暗中开场；细雨蒙蒙，车流轰鸣，镜头环摇过一组弧形的玻璃幕墙办公楼，楼内灯光昏暗。画面转向其中一栋楼的入口，我们听到清晨的鸟鸣。外面仍然黑着，穿牛仔裤和夹克的女人们开始穿过巨大的玻璃门，走进门厅。她们进入时，我们听到一连串名字：安杰拉、安杰利卡、佐尔蒂、埃尔维拉、玛丽亚娜、索菲娅、戈尔达娜、德拉加娜、米尔卡、巴尔塔、莉迪娅、米格蕾塔，还有更多。镜头跳转到一条长长的后勤走廊，头顶是红色管道，随后又转向一间空更衣室，里面有窄长凳和整齐排列的实用鞋与运动鞋；鞋的主人们已换上制服，开始值班。穿着白T恤、系着海军蓝与白色条纹围裙的女人们在一间储藏室里，把按颜色编码的抹布装进灰色塑料托盘。她们默默地做着这项工作，每个人都专注于例行事务。装好清洁用品后，她们把灰色塑料托盘叠起来，系上背带，然后沿走廊返回。清洁团队出发时，一队厨房员工从旁经过，她们戴着塑料发罩，推着摆满托盘和餐饮设备的金属推车。
en: The film opens in the dark; there is light drizzle and the roar of traffic as the camera pans around a series of curved, glass- fronted office blocks, their lights dimmed. The view shifts to the entrance to one of the blocks, and we hear early-morning bird song. It is still dark outside, when women in jeans and jackets begin to walk through the large glass doors and into the lobby. As they enter, we hear a rollcall of names: Angela, Angelika, Zolti, Elvira, Marijana, Sofia, Gordana, Dragana, Milka, Balta, Lidia, Migreta, and more. The camera jumps to a long service corridor with red pipes overhead and then to an empty locker room, with narrow benches and neat rows of practical shoes and trainers; their owners have changed into uniforms and are beginning their shifts. Women in white T-shirts and navy-and-white striped aprons are in a storeroom, loading grey plastic trays with colour-coded cloths. They go about this work silently, each focused on the routine. Having loaded up with cleaning supplies, they stack the grey plastic trays and attach carry straps before heading back up the corridor. As the cleaning team heads out, a team of kitchen staff pass by, wearing plastic hair coverings and wheeling metal trolleys ranged with trays and catering equipment.

zh: 画面渐变为刺眼的白，一位面容和善、深色头发别在耳后的中年女人在素净背景前特写出现，微微一笑。出人意料的是，她用母语背诵了一首诗的三个诗行。她面部的镜头淡出，我们读到英文插字幕：“我从南方来／无论我去往何处／苔藓总跟着我”。背景中，物件碰撞的声响持续不断，像劳动的合唱。另一位女人接着上场，说出她的诗句：她也是中年，这次是金发，戴着耳环，微笑着，带着浓重的斯拉夫口音，微微出汗。她穿着同样的制服。插字幕传达一种惬意的休息状态：“星期天来临时／我躺在荫影里／那是我家谱树的荫影”，尽管最后一行“我是那根折断的树枝”带有一丝忧郁和孤立感。然而，当我们试图欣赏这诗时，吸尘器发出震耳欲聋的嗡鸣，令人不快地持续着，与诗所传达的平静状态形成鲜明对比。
en: The screen fades to a blinding white and a middle-aged woman with pleasant features and dark hair tucked behind her ears is shown close up against a plain background, smiling lightly. Unexpectedly, she recites three lines of a poem in her native language. The shot of her face fades out and we read the English intertitle: ‘I came from the South / Wherever I go / the moss keeps following me’. In the background, the sound of objects clattering about continues like a chorus of labour. Another woman takes her turn, and says her piece: she is also middle-aged, this time blonde, with earrings, smiling, in a deep Slavonic accent, slightly perspiring. She wears the same uniform. The intertitle conveys a pleasurable state of rest: ‘When Sunday comes / I lie down in the shade / Of my family tree’, though this is tinged with melancholy and a sense of isolation in the final line, which reads: ‘I am the branch that broke off’. As we try to appreciate the poetry, though, there is a deafening drone of hoovering, unpleasantly insistent and in stark contrast with the state of calm conveyed by the poem.

zh: 建筑外景显示，穿制服的清洁女工在每一层工作，日出映照在弧形建筑群的玻璃楼层中。开放式设计中设有数百个工作位，每个都有各自的清洁难题。清洁是全身性的工作，女人们执行各种各样的任务：推车、吸尘、掸灰。她们伸手越过圆桌擦拭桌面；俯身清洁桌下，一只手拉出椅子，另一只手引导吸尘器；擦净每一种可想象的表面——桌子、椅子、椅背、橱柜、咖啡桌、复印机、马桶（座圈、座圈背面、圈缘下方、底座周围）、水槽、水龙头、镜子；从洗碗机中取出餐具，把餐具摆上架子；更换垃圾袋。在食堂厨房里，穿白T恤、套蓝色一次性塑料围裙、戴黑手套的女人们在传送带上工作，分拣盘子、托盘、杯子，把食物残渣刮进垃圾桶；那里是一片不停歇的活动蜂巢。在洗碗机的另一侧，更多女人把干净餐具分类堆放并运走。工作单调乏味，而传送带不停运转这一事实使其变得无休无止。一些系橙色围裙的男人在相邻空间工作，也许是厨房搬运工。许多被清洁的空间是混合性与辅助性空间，而非严格意义上的工作空间：白领员工的公共休息室，摆放矮桌和报纸的休息处。桌子已为早晨的会议摆好，咖啡杯和瓶装水准备就绪，舒适而有品位的办公椅，与窗外晨光中的城市景观一样诱人。女人们使用各式各样的旋转拖把和清洁用品，从粉色清洁液到外科手套。她们以大幅度的动作来回、打圈擦拭，打磨到一切闪闪发亮。她们填写清洁记录表，注明厕所已清洁。随着清洁推进，太阳升起，白天到来：白领员工和客户开始抵达。当他们到达时，清洁女工正在擦拭玻璃旋转门。
en: An exterior view of the building reveals uniformed cleaners working on every floor, as the sunrise is reflected in the glass stories of the curved complex. There are hundreds of workstations in the open-plan design, each with its own cleaning challenges. The cleaning is full body work and the women perform a wide range of tasks: wheeling trolleys, hoovering, dusting. They reach across round tables to wipe them; lean down to clean underneath desks, pulling out chairs with one hand and directing the hoover with the other; wipe down every imaginable surface – tables, chairs, backs of chairs, cupboards coffee tables, photocopiers, toilets (seats, backs of seats, under the rims, around the pedestals), sinks, taps, mirrors; unload dishwashers, stack crockery on shelves; change bin-liners. Women in white T-shirts in blue plastic disposable aprons and black gloves work on a conveyer belt in the kitchens of the canteen, sorting plates, trays, cups, scraping remains of food into bins; it is a hive of relentless activity. On the other side of the dishwasher, more women sort clean crockery into piles and take it away. The work is monotonous and made relentless by the fact it is a conveyer belt that just keeps going. Some men in orange aprons work in the adjacent space, perhaps as kitchen porters. Many of the spaces being cleaned are hybrid and auxiliary spaces rather than workspaces per se: common rooms for the white-collar workers, resting places with low tables and newspapers. Tables are set up for the morning’s meetings, coffee cups and bottled waters at the ready, comfortable tasteful office chairs as inviting as the view of the city in the morning sunshine beyond. The women wield all manner of swivel-mops and products, from pink cleaning fluid to surgical gloves. They wipe with sweeping movements to and fro, round and round, polishing until everything gleams. Time sheets are filled out to show that the toilets have been cleaned. As the cleaning progresses, the sun rises and it is daytime: the white collar workers and clients begin to arrive. As they do, the cleaning women polish the glass turn-style doors.

zh: 摄影机无声见证着这片在条形灯光下展开的大量活动。垃圾与污垢只在被消失的过程中被短暂瞥见。镜头角度聚焦于女人们双手的灵巧，以及她们熟练动作的细微之处。她们常常优雅如舞的动作，仿佛经过编排，与建筑相流动：她们沿着宽敞的楼梯往下走、边走边拖地时，场景从下方拍摄。白色门厅那些微缩的尼迈耶式曲线，与接待台流线型的金属带相得益彰；接待台上装饰着一排新鲜红色剑兰的花瓶。其他空间也点缀着盆栽和炫耀性的企业花艺（无疑是通过一系列分包商采购的）。繁多的室内设计元素与照明装置争相吸引我们的注意：天花板上点缀着星系般的LED灯，还有立柱、圆形悬浮墙，而相似却不同的空间之间的通道似乎没有尽头。镜头似乎在嘲弄所有这些品味上的努力，更感兴趣的是待清洁的大量表面。影片中有一处，一位女人在典型地宽阔的空间（12层高管会议区）吸尘。背景中，我们看到一张投影照片：一个高大、裸体、秃顶的男人——萨格勒布艺术家托米斯拉夫·戈托瓦茨，出自他的影像作品《守望莱茵河》（

，1994），作于南斯拉夫战争期间；他在这件作品中花数小时眺望萨格勒布城，站在克罗地亚艺术家协会屋顶上充当“清真寺守卫”的哨兵（该建筑曾在1940年代被穆斯林社群用作清真寺）。当代的清洁女工照常工作，仿佛那影像并不存在，忽略那个越过她望去的裸体男人——他的目光越过上方，投向远处的城市。摄影机穿行建筑的段落伴随着嗖嗖擦洗与咔嗒声响构成的打击乐：拖把在抛光混凝土地面上划出无尽的圈，吸尘器嗡鸣，餐具叮当作响，而这一切都弥漫着一种安静的电子滋滋声。这是一个完全人造的工作环境，清洁工的大量劳动发生在无窗的混凝土与金属后勤区域，与办公空间中大量的木材和玻璃形成对比。值班结束时，伊韦科维奇镜头中的女人们把清洁抹布放进两台大型洗烘一体机：右侧放粉色和黄色抹布，左侧放蓝色和绿色抹布。想必不同抹布用于不同工作，但人们也感到伊韦科维奇或许在此还作出一种艺术类比：她们的劳动和她的劳动一样涉及审美选择，尽管方式极为不同。往机器里装填抹布，让我们想到下一班接班的工人：她们会先取出这些洗好的抹布，再次启动整个日常循环。
en: The camera plays silent witness to this mass of strip-lit activity. Waste and dirt are glimpsed only fleetingly, in the process of being disappeared. The camera angles focus on the manual dexterity of the women and the minutiae of their expert movements. Their often graceful, dance-like movements appear choreographed to flow with the architecture: scenes are shot from below as they make their way down the generous staircases, mopping as they go. The micro-Niemeyerian curves of the white lobby are complemented by the aerodynamic metal swathe of a welcome desk, adorned with a series of vases of fresh red gladioli. Other spaces are also dotted with potted plants and ostentatious corporate flower arrangements (doubtless procured through a series of subcontractors). A plethora of internal design features and lighting fixtures vie for our attention: the ceilings are dotted with a galaxy of LED lights, there are columns, circular floating walls, and the passage between the similar but different spaces seems endless. The camera seems to mock all these efforts at taste, more interested in the masses of surfaces to be cleaned. At one point in the film a woman is shown hoovering a characteristically expansive space (Executive Meeting Area, Level 12). In the background we see a projected photo of a tall, naked, balding man – Zagreb artist Tomislav Gotovac, in his video piece

(1994), made during the Yugoslav wars, which involved him spending hours looking across the city of Zagreb, standing sentry as a ‘mosque guard’ on the roof of the Croatian Association of Artists (once used as a mosque by the Muslim community in the 1940s). The contemporary cleaner goes about her work as though the image were not there, ignoring the naked man looking past her, his gaze directed above and away, to the city beyond. The passage of the camera through the building is accompanied by a percussion of swish-swashing and clicking as mops make endless loops of polished concrete floors, while hoovers drone and dishes clatter, all pervaded by a quiet electronic buzz. It is an entirely artificial working environment and much of the cleaners’ labour takes place in windowless concrete and metal service areas, in contrast to the abundance of wood and glass in the office spaces. At the end of their shift, Iveković’s subjects put their cleaning cloths into two large washer dryers: pink and yellow cloths on the right, blue and green cloths on the left. Presumably the different cloths are for different jobs, though one senses Iveković may also be drawing an artistic analogy here too: their labour, like hers, is involved with aesthetic choices, though in very different ways. The loading of the machines reminds us of those that will come on in the next shift, and begin by unloading these same, washed cloths, to restart the whole daily cycle once more.

zh: 工人们受雇，以不可见的方式抹去其他工人的痕迹，让一栋气派的玻璃幕墙建筑看起来像新的一样。这一情境呼应了杰夫·沃尔的摄影作品《晨间清洁，密斯·凡·德·罗基金会，巴塞罗那》（1999）所精心布置的场景：一名有色人种正在擦拭这座标志性玻璃建筑的地面，而庭院后方一尊古典裸体雕塑炫耀着其理想化的白色形体。或许症候性的是，泰特美术馆网站对该作品的解读起初聚焦于图像的形式构图，似乎避开了“清洁工”一词，而把这位工人先称为“服务人员”，随后称为“看管者”：
en: The workers are paid to invisibly erase the traces of other workers and to make a prestigious glass-fronted building look as good as new. The situation echoes that staged so well in Jeff Wall’s photograph

children: Morning Cleaning Mies van der Rohe Foundation

en: (1999), in which a person of colour is seen mopping the floor of the iconic glass building, while a classical nude sculpture flaunts its idealized white form in the courtyard behind. Symptomatically, perhaps, the Tate website’s interpretation of the piece initially focuses on the formal composition of the images and appears to shrink from the term ‘cleaner’, referring to the worker, instead, as first an ‘attendant’ and then as a ‘custodian’:

zh: 在清晨明亮的光线中，可见陈设极简的空间。前景中，一根闪亮的钢柱几乎把构图垂直分成两半。钢柱之外，越过一大片深色地毯，一名服务人员正在清洁一面玻璃板墙。晨光照亮建筑清晰利落的线条，同时在左侧一面纹理很深的缟玛瑙墙上投下明显的阴影。在看管者准备清洁的玻璃板上，流下的水在对称图案的玻璃表面形成随意图案，部分遮住一个庭院，那里有一尊格奥尔格·科尔贝（1877—1947）的女性裸体雕塑立在池畔。
en: The minimally-furnished space is seen in the bright light of early  morning. In the foreground, a gleaming steel pillar divides the  composition vertically almost in half. Beyond the pillar, across an  expanse of dark carpet, an attendant is in the process of cleaning a  glass-panelled wall. The morning sun illuminates the clear and crisp  lines of the building’s architecture, while producing pronounced  shadows on a deeply veined onyx wall to the left. On the panels the  custodian has prepared for cleaning, streaming water adds a random  design onto the surface of the symmetrically-patterned glass, which  partially obscures a courtyard where a sculpture of a female nude by  Georg Kolbe (1877–1947) stands by a pond.

zh: 密斯建筑的形式严谨传达一种简洁感，并沉溺于材料的纯粹，而清洁工的劳动则指向维持“少即是多”幻觉所需的努力。沃尔指出：“清洁是神秘的……因为它是那种如果成功就会抹除自身的劳动。”他评论道：“［这些］建筑需要格外一丝不苟的维护。在更传统的空间里，一点灰尘和污垢并不构成对整体概念如此刺眼的对比。它甚至可以变成包浆，但这些密斯式建筑尽其所能抵抗包浆。”
en: Whilst the Mies building’s formal rigour conveys a sense of simplicity and luxuriates in the purity of materials, the cleaner’s labour points to the effort entailed in maintaining an illusion of ‘less’ as ‘more’. Wall has noted that ‘Cleaning is mysterious … since it is the labour that erases itself if it is successful.’ He observes: ‘[These] buildings require an especially scrupulous level of maintenance. In more traditional spaces a little dirt and grime is not such a shocking contrast to the whole concept. It can even become patina, but these Miesian buildings resist patina as much as they can.’

zh: 在伊韦科维奇整部影片中，劳动场景不断被女人们的特写打断。摄影机在她们脸上停留长达一分钟，产生一种让人想起安迪·沃霍尔著名“试镜”系列的效果。沃霍尔有一句名言：“银幕魅力是一种秘密。如果你能弄明白它是什么、如何制造它，你就有了一个真正能卖的好产品。但在你真正看到某个人出现在银幕上之前，你甚至无法判断他有没有这种魅力。你必须通过试镜来发现。”

在我看来，埃斯特园区的清洁女工即使不是全部，也有许多颇具银幕魅力。当我们看着她们在明亮白光下接受摄影机的审视时，她们的面孔展现出中欧、东欧和南欧“类型”的多样性：从金发蓝眼、宽脸高颧骨，到肤色较深、黑发油亮的人。有些年轻，有些年长，很可能已经做了祖母。我们不禁想到，较年轻的人是否会把整个职业生涯都花在类似的岗位上。如果说沃霍尔声称“我只想找到很棒的人，让他们做自己……然后拍他们一定长度的时间，那就是电影”，
那么伊韦科维奇镜头下的女人则汇聚成一个合唱队，围绕一位女性主义诗人的诗句团结起来。
en: Throughout Iveković’s film, the scenes of labour are interrupted by close-up shots of the women. The camera lingers on their faces for up to a minute, producing an effect reminiscent of Andy Warhol’s famous series of ‘screen tests’. Warhol famously claimed that ‘screen magnetism is something secret. If you could figure out what it is and how you make it, you’d have a really good product to sell. But you can’t even tell if someone has it until you actually see them up there on the screen. You have to give screen tests to find out.’

Many, if not all, of the Erste Campus cleaning women seem magnetic to me. As we watch them subject themselves to the scrutiny of the camera under bright white light, their faces demonstrate a diversity of central, eastern and southern European ‘types’, from blonde and blue-eyed with wide faces and high cheekbones to others with darker complexions and glossy black hair. Some are young, some are older, likely already grandmothers. We wonder whether the younger ones will spend their whole working lives in similar roles. If Warhol claimed ‘I only wanted to find great people and let them be themselves … and I’d film them for a certain length of time and that would be the movie’,
Iveković’s individual women come together to form a chorus, rallying around the words of a feminist poet.

zh: 因为伊韦科维奇的女人们不像沃霍尔的被摄者那样沉默，尽管她们说出的话也不完全属于自己。她们用别人的词，却以自己的语言说话；她们选择自己要背诵的诗行，这些诗行选自艾达·巴吉奇的诗歌，从克罗地亚语译成她们的母语，每人几行。聆听时，人们会为她们声音的不同质感以及构成各种语言的声音多样性所打动。我们也许能辨认出其中一些是斯拉夫语言，另一些则感觉较为陌生。与伊韦科维奇合作的这组女性是波斯尼亚人、克罗地亚人、科索沃人、波兰人、罗马尼亚人、塞尔维亚人和土耳其人。她们有些人像女学生那样背诵，有些人像初露头角的女演员；有些女人背诵得清晰自信，另一些更害羞、有些局促，不习惯摄影机的关注，但她们都念完了自己的诗句，看上去松了口气，甚至可能有些自豪。所有人都似乎为念完诗行而高兴，许多人露出微笑。她们所选的文本显得极为个人化，令观者想了解她们的人生故事，以及她们怎么会来到维也纳清洁这家银行。每个人都被鼓励选择自己在某种方式上感到共鸣的诗行。
en: For Iveković’s women are not silent like Warhol’s sitters, though neither are the words they speak entirely their own. They speak the words of another but in their own languages, and they have chosen their own lines to recite, selected from the poetry of Aida Bagić, translated from Croatian into their native tongues, a few lines each. Listening, one is struck by the different qualities of their voices and the diversity of sounds that make up the various languages. We may recognize some as Slavonic; others may feel less familiar. The group of women Iveković worked with were Bosnian, Croatian, Kosovan, Polish, Romanian, Serbian and Turkish. Some of them recite like schoolgirls, some like budding actresses; some of the women recite clearly and confidently, others are more shy, a little embarrassed and not used to the attention of the camera, but they all get through their lines and look relieved and perhaps even a little proud. All seem pleased to come to the end of their lines, and many smile. Their selections of text seem highly personal and make the viewer wonder about their life stories and how it came to be that they are working at cleaning the bank, in Vienna. Each has been encouraged to choose lines to which she felt connected to in some way.

zh: 有些诗句似乎追忆更艰难的时光：“失忆不是一种病症／它是一种解药／用来对抗那一刻的记忆／当一切开始走下坡路／如果我记不起来”。许多是日常的，却以某种方式指示着微小的满足，以及一种一切井然有序的感觉：“我天亮前离家／城市安静／面包已烤好”；“我四点半起床／电车不挤／于是我睡在温暖里”；“我有一座小花园／除草占据我全部注意力／每一片草叶都独一无二”；“我天亮前起床／看云、人们和／瓶中信漂过／然后我看看自己／手掌，我看见／一切都会好的”。它们提供实用的生存建议：“我母亲告诉我／别花那么多时间／待在自己脑子里／你最好到外面去。到新鲜空气里／我母亲是个聪明的女人。”考虑到清洁工作是在室内接触化学品，这一建议的讽刺意味显而易见。有几句涉及女性劳动的性质：“女人的工作／永远做不完／我刚做完／就感觉自己还没开始”；“人们说女人撑着／房子的三个角／但我清洁全部四个角”；也许是以男人的口吻说——“女人能做到／我也能做到／各种各样的事我都能做／但我不必做，所以我不会做”。另一些涉及等待邮件：“我向邮递员挥手／但他们不认识我／因为我不是从这里来的／我是从那里来的／我随风而来／也将随风而去”；“我一直在等一封信／已经好几个月了／邮递员后来对我说／我不知道那是你”。最后引用的句子是“我不知道那是你”，也许呼应了这些女人本身不被了解、不被承认这一意味——正如伊韦科维奇的标题所暗示的，她们是“不可见的”。
en: Some of the lines of poetry seem to hark back to harder times: ‘Loss of memory is not a disorder / It is a remedy / Against memories of the moment / when everything started to go downhill / If I cannot remember it’. Many are day-to-day, yet somehow indicative of small satisfactions, and a sense that things are in order: ‘I leave the house before dawn / The city is quiet / the bread is baked’; ‘I get up at half past four / trams are not crowded / so I sleep in the warm’; ‘I have a small garden / Weeding takes my full attention / Each blade of grass is unique’; ‘I get up before dawn / And I watch clouds people and / bottled messages go by / Then I look at the palm of / my hand and I see / It will be alright’. They offer practical advice for getting by: ‘My mother tells me / Don’t spent that much time / inside your head / You’re better off outside. In the fresh air / My mother is a wise woman’. The irony of this advice, in view of the indoor chemical nature of the cleaning work is clear. Several lines address the nature of female labour: ‘A woman’s work is / never done / As soon as I finish / it feels as if I haven’t even started’; ‘They say a woman holds / three corners of the house / But I clean all four’; perhaps in the voice of a man – ‘Women can do it / I can do it too / I can do all kinds of things / But I don’t have to, so I won’t’. Others refer to the experience of waiting for the mail: ‘I wave to the postmen / But they do not know me / Because I am not from here / I am from there / I came with the wind / And with wind I will go’; ‘I’ve been waiting for a letter / for months now / The postman later said to me / I didn’t know it was you’. The last line cited is ‘I didn’t know it was you’, perhaps echoing the sense in which the women themselves are not known, not recognized, ‘invisible’ as Iveković’s title implies.

zh: 离家的距离是一个关键主题：“我的生活会轻松许多／如果我一只手握雨／另一只手握太阳／那我就不必去任何地方。”

一些核心诗句像叠句一样被重复，因为它们被不止一次选中。值得注意的是，这些是涉及流离失所经验以及坚持伦理的诗句：“我不是从这里来的／我是从那里来的／我随风而来／我将随风而去”。有几位女人，尤其是那些年长者——她们的眼神比更年轻、更乐观的同事更悲伤、更受压制——重复这些诗句：“跌倒，起来。／再次跌倒。／起来。／跌倒。／如果你每天练习／跌倒很容易”。较年轻的女人往往是选择更浪漫诗句的人；年长者则选择更忧郁的诗句，不过跌倒、起来、再次跌倒的问题，也可能像萨缪尔·贝克特在《向着更糟去》中的箴言“无所谓。再试一次。再失败一次。失败得更好”一样，是一种行动号召。这是伊韦科维奇过去自己也曾处理过的主题，尤其是在名为《练习造就大师》（1982）的影像表演中。在这件作品中，一位穿黑色晚礼服的女性相当僵硬地站在舞台上的摄影机前，头上套着白色塑料袋。突然，她身体一震，倒在地上。过了一会儿。她一动不动地躺着。然后，她站起来，再次站在舞台上。她身体猛然一震，仿佛被枪杀，又倒了下去。这一动作循环重复。女人跌倒，爬起，再跌倒，再起来。在另一件重要的合作作品《女性之家》（2009）中，伊韦科维奇与来自一家庇护所的女性合作——她们离开了暴力关系以重建生活——并为她们的面部制作石膏翻模；这些面具后来被转化成一个肃穆的陵墓，一圈由翻模面孔组成的肖像安装在基座上。每个面具下方记录了其主人的故事。这些女人及其孩子的故事读来令人悲伤。虽然每个故事都不同，但其中描述的暴力关系的动力机制从根本上相同，而且显然家庭暴力折磨着所有国籍和年龄群体：玛丽亚，51岁，葡萄牙人，已婚，一个孩子；蕾妮，35岁，卢森堡人，已婚，三个孩子；法蒂玛，24岁，佛得角人，已婚……名单还在继续。正如玛丽亚·赫拉瓦约娃所论证的，伊韦科维奇对这类新合作实践形式的拥抱，用艺术家自己的话说，旨在“不仅阐明政治论点，从而使已经知道它的人明白，而且把艺术纳入政治实践，形成新观念并将其传播到社会中”。
en: Distance from home is a key theme: ‘My life would be so easy / If I had rain in one hand / and the sun in the other / Then I wouldn’t need to go anywhere’.

A number of core lines are repeated like a refrain, having been selected more than once. Notably these are those that relate to the experience of displacement: ‘I am not from here / I am from there / I came with the wind / With the wind I will go’, as well as to an ethic of perseverance. Several of the women, particularly those who are older, their eyes sadder, more browbeaten than their younger, more optimistic colleagues, repeat the lines ‘Fall down, get up. / Fall down again. / Get up. / Fall down. / Falling comes easy if you / practice every day’. The younger women tend to be the ones who chose the more romantic lines; the older ones those more melancholic, though the question of falling down, getting up and falling down again, might also be a call to action, along the lines of Samuel Beckett’s mantra ‘No matter. Try again. Fail Again. Fail Better’ from
It is a topic Iveković has addressed herself in the past, notably in a video performance entitled

(1982). Here, a woman in a black evening dress is shown standing rather stiffly on the stage before the camera, hooded with a white plastic bag. Suddenly her body jolts and she collapses to the ground. Some time passes. She lies immobile. Then, she gets up, and stands on the stage again. Her body jolts as though she had been shot dead, and she collapses again. The action is repeated, on a loop. Women fall, pick themselves up, fall again, get up again. In another major collaborative work,

(2009), Iveković worked with women from a shelter, who had left violent relationships to rebuild their lives, and made plaster casts of their faces, which were later transformed into an austere mausoleum in a circle of cast faces, installed on plinths. Its owner’s stories were recorded beneath each mask. The stories of these women and their children make sad reading. While every story is different, the dynamics of the violent relationships described in each are fundamentally the same, and it is clear that domestic violence afflicts all nationalities and age groups: Maria, 51, Portuguese, married, one child; Renee, 35, Luxembourger, married, three children; Fatima, 24, Cap Verdese, married… the list goes on. As Maria Hlavajova has argued, Iveković’s embrace of new forms of collaborative practice like these seeks, as the artist has herself put it, ‘not just to illustrate the political thesis, thus making it clear to those who already know it, but to include art into the political praxis, form new ideas and spread them into society’.

zh: 然而，正如曼努埃拉·博亚齐耶夫与塞尔哈特·卡拉卡亚勒所论证的，必须警惕这样一种程度：“尤其是在左派中间……与主要是移民的‘他者’团结的表达，不仅使自己的‘自身’位置免于质疑，而且把‘可怜的他人’受害者化，剥夺他们自身采取政治行动的能力。”
因此，问题应当由“所有那些”像他们一样“不再相信移民斗争是历史附戏的人”提出：“如果并且当移民跨越边界时……他们……已经（并以一种新的方式）成为民族与全球社会关系的一部分，而他们自己也改变这些关系。”他们坚持认为，“移民的主体性不可还原为其劳动力角色”。

在我看来，这正是伊韦科维奇邀请清洁女工选择并朗诵诗歌时所努力展示的，关键在于这些诗被译成她们自己的语言；而不是把合作者化约为基本人口统计资料——《女性之家》项目在文献记录中的后续呈现也许不可避免地部分如此。尽管这些诗句在某些情况下可能与女人们的劳动、与清洁的经验产生联系，但在这个意义上它们不可还原：它们还暗示过去与未来、渴望、梦想，以及共同的移民经验；这种经验对于今日欧洲现实的性质及其体验仍然至关重要：无论1989年及向后社会主义的“转型”所加速的境况变化与新的经济社会不平等如何，它都是如此；而与此同时，也恰恰是这些变化与不平等，使这一经验如此重要。
en: Nevertheless, as Manuela Bojadzijev and Serhat Karakayali have argued, it is essential to be mindful of the degree to which, ‘particularly among leftists … expressions of solidarity with the mostly migrant “others” not only leave one’s “own” position unquestioned, but also victimise the “poor others” and deny them their own capacity for political action’.

And questions should therefore be posed by ‘all those who’, like them, ‘no longer believe the struggles of migration to be a sideshow of history’: ‘if and when migrants cross borders … they … are already (and then, in a new way) a part of national and global social relations, which they also themselves transform’. They insist that ‘the subjectivity of migrants is not reducible to their role as labour-power’.

This, it seems to me, is what Iveković strives to demonstrate when she invites the cleaners to select and recite poetry, crucially, translated into their own languages; rather than reduce her collaborators to vital statistics, as was, perhaps inevitably, in part the case in the documentary afterlife of the

project. While the lines of poetry may be relatable, in some cases, to the women’s experience of labour, to cleaning, they are not reducible in this sense: they also allude to the past and future, to longing, to dreams, and to the shared experience of migration, which remains so central to the nature and experience of European reality today, both irrespective of and yet also precisely because of the changed circumstances and new economic and social inequalities accelerated by 1989 and the ‘transition’ to post-socialism.

zh: 甚至在新冠疫情之前，弗朗索瓦丝·韦尔热斯就写道，我们生活在“一个对干净的艺术、干净的水、干净的房屋、干净的身体、干净的心灵和绿色空间的关切日益增长的时代”。她论证说，这是“1970年代新时代意识形态的延伸”，也是一种市场的延伸，而该市场的“目标是个人效率以及身体与精神力量的最大化”。她写到“清洁与肮脏之间被划出的新边界”，解释说新自由主义白人男性的表演性身体从根本上由“不可见身体……女性和有色人种”支撑，而后者的疲惫反过来仍是“提取主义历史逻辑的后果，这种逻辑构建了原始积累与资本——从被种族化的身体中提取劳动”；她得出结论：“有色人种女性清洁工作的不可见性，创造了干净家庭和公共空间的可见性。”因此，她论证说，今天的清洁是一项更长久的历史性“
”的一部分。她指出，清洁女工“谈到自己睡的时间很少……谈到花在通勤上的漫长小时，以及回家后还必须做的工作”。

完全相同的一点，已在伯威克街电影集体1975年的影片《夜间清洁工》（第一部分，90分钟）中得到明确表达；该片致力于提高人们对清洁工劳动的认识，并记录她们争取工会化的运动。片中一系列女性被令人难忘地询问“你能睡上觉吗？”，她们以就事论事的口吻讲述——仿佛惊讶于竟然有人想知道——如何在哄孩子入睡与出门上夜班之间平均每晚抢睡一个半小时。正如西奥娜·威尔逊等人所概述的，夜间清洁工运动“挑战了有组织左派内部更深层的一套排斥”，并“试图界定一种超越中产阶级女性经验范围、把工人阶级和移民女性包括在内的女性主义政治”。
en: Even before Covid-19, Françoise Vergès had written that we lived in ‘an age in which concerns are growing for clean art, clean water, clean houses, clean bodies, clean minds and green space’. This was, she argued, ‘an extension of New Age ideology of the 1970s’ and of a market whose ‘aim is personal efficiency and a maximization of physical and mental power’. She wrote of ‘new borders that have been drawn between cleanliness and dirtiness’, explaining how the performing body of the neoliberal white male was fundamentally undergirded by the ‘invisible body ... female and a person of color’, whose exhaustion, in turn, remains ‘the consequence of the historical logic of extractivism that built primitive accumulation and capital – extracting labor from racialised bodies’; concluding that ‘invisibility of the cleaning jobs of women of color creates the visibility of clean homes and public spaces’. Thus, she argues, cleaning, today, is part of a longer, historical ‘
’. Cleaning women, she noted, ‘speak of the very little time they sleep … of the long hours devoted to their commutes, and of the work they have to do once they return home’.
The very same point was already made explicit in the 1975 film

, 90 mins) by the Berwick Street Film Collective, devoted to raising recognition of the labour of cleaners and documenting the campaign for their unionization, in which a series of women are memorably asked ‘Do you get any sleep?’, and recount, in matter-of-fact tones, as though surprised that anyone is even interested to know, how they try to snatch an average of an hour and a half per might, between putting their babies to bed and heading out for their night shifts. As Siona Wilson, among others, has outlined, the night cleaners’ campaign ‘challenged a deeper set of expulsions within the organized left’ and ‘sought to define a feminist politics that went beyond the confines of middle-class women’s experience to include working-class and immigrant women*’*.

zh: 伊韦科维奇追随这一早期女性主义项目的足迹，邀请奥地利工会联合会下属工会VIDA的代表（乌尔苏拉·沃迪奇卡）与埃斯特园区的清洁女工交谈，并向她们解释奥地利关于职工委员会的法律。谈话记录显示，女人们挣的是每小时8.36欧元的最低工资，而且自新大楼大约五个月前启用以来，她们一直在那里工作。沃迪奇卡向女人们解释为什么职工委员会重要：“如果大家联合起来、组织起来，就能改善状况。”她说：“需要像你们这样的人告诉我们问题在哪里、你们担心什么、你们有哪些恐惧、需要哪些帮助。”

她告诉她们，“职工委员会可以帮助向老板提出各种各样的问题”，从清洁用品的质量或机器的效率，到尝试为有育儿责任的员工协商更合适的工作时间，再到确保如果老板想裁减员工，委员会可以帮助决定谁较有条件在被裁后找到新工作等等。她解释说，委员会大约可以在两个月内成立，并谈到程序与成员规则，讨论自我组织以及如何挑选和选举代表的问题。她在语言与沟通问题对她这类组织的重要性上停留了一阵。她说，重要的是，代表清洁工与老板谈判的人要德语说得好，否则不会被认真对待。她说，她的工会致力于与清洁女工沟通、努力理解她们的关切，以克服这群时间匮乏、讲许多种不同母语、德语熟练程度各异的女性所面临的不可避免的语言障碍。
en: Iveković follows in the footsteps of this earlier feminist project, when she invites a representative from the trade union VIDA, part of the Austrian Trade Union Federation (Ursula Woditscha) to speak with the cleaning women at Erste Campus and to explain Austrian laws about workers’ council’s with them. The notes from the conversation record that the women earned the minimum rate of €8.36 and that they had been working in the new building since it opened approximately some five months before. Woditscha explained to the women why a work council is important, explaining: ‘If everyone gets together and gets organized, you can improve things.’ She says: ‘people like you who tell us where the problems lie, what worries you, which fears you have and which help you need.’

She tells them that ‘the council can help raise all sorts of issues with the bosses’, ranging from the quality of cleaning products or the efficiency of machines, to trying to negotiate more suitable working hours for staff with childcare responsibilities, to ensuring that if the boss wants to reduce the number of staff the council can help decide who is best placed to find a new job and to be laid off, and so on. She explains that a council can be formed in around two months and talks about the procedure and membership rules, discussing issues around self-organization and how to select and elect a representative. She lingers for a while on the importance of issues around language and communication in an organization like hers. It is important, she says, that those sent to negotiate on the cleaners’ behalf with the bosses speak good German, otherwise they will not be taken seriously. Her union, she says, is committed to communicating with the cleaners and to trying to understand their concerns, to overcome the inevitable language barriers faced by a time-poor group of women speaking many different home languages with differing levels of German proficiency.

zh: 当邀请女人们提问时，有人问及获得医疗服务的途径，解释说她们被告知可以使用埃斯特的医疗服务，但从未见过相关代表：“某个地方写着埃斯特集团有医生，但我们从没见过这个人。”
en: When the women were invited to ask questions, one asked about access to healthcare, explaining that they had been told that they had access to Erste healthcare but had not met any representatives about it: ‘Somewhere it is written that we have a doctor at the Erste Group, but we have never seen this person.’

zh: 沃迪奇卡指出，由于清洁工作被分包，严格来说这些女人是另一家公司——此处是一家名为蒙多（Mundo）的公司——的雇员，而非埃斯特的直接雇员，这可能影响她们获得医疗服务。尽管约有4,500名埃斯特员工在园区工作，清洁工作当然已被外包，成为庞大商业清洁服务市场的一部分；在这个市场中，雇主承担更少风险，雇员领取更低工资，中间商拿走大部分利益。正如赫尔马·卢茨所论证的：“雇主喜欢把家政工人视为服务提供者；这大体上是一种开脱性修辞，方便地把辩论从权力与依赖关系中转移开，因为（受过学术教育的）中上层阶级客户通常知道，自己并非一项受法律保障的服务提供合同的当事方。”
伊韦科维奇对工人状况的田野调查所产生的一个结果，直接来自工会代表与清洁女工之间的问答。项目结束时，这些女性尽管身份是间接雇员，仍获得了使用埃斯特园区健康中心的权利。
en: Woditscha points out that as the cleaning is subcontracted, the women are technically employees of another company, in this case one called Mundo, rather than Erste directly, and that this may have implications for their access to healthcare. While there are around 4,500 Erste employees working on campus, cleaning has of course been contracted out, part of a massive commercial cleaning service market, which sees employers take less risk, employees take lower wages, and middlemen take the lion’s share of the benefits. As Helma Lutz has argued: ‘Employers like to see their domestic workers as service providers; it is largely a form of exculpatory rhetoric which conveniently diverts the debate away from relations of power and dependence, since the (academically) educated upper-middle class clients will usually know that they are not party to a legally safeguarded service-provider contract.’

One of the outcomes of Iveković’s field research into the workers’ conditions was a direct result of the Q&A between the union representative and the cleaners. On conclusion of the project, the women gained access to the health centre on the Erste campus, despite their status as indirect employees.

zh: 在一个力图成为新式“企业文化”典范的园区拍摄清洁工，伊韦科维奇凸显了所谓“非物质”与“物质”劳动者之间的相互依赖，并把后者持续被视作理所当然的种种方式推到前景。凯蒂·丘赫罗夫观察到，“‘非物质劳动者’这一‘阶级’内部的阶级鸿沟极其巨大”，因为“大部分非物质劳动工作者完全用不上自己的高等教育，并在专业之外工作”。此外，她有力地反驳了当代艺术界的一个神话：“‘革命性’词汇和‘无产阶级’诗学主要出现在当代批评与创意产业的话语中，很少出现在不受尊崇的物质劳动领域。”鉴于这些及其他有问题的预设，她指出：
en: In filming cleaners on a campus that set out to make itself a model for a new form of ‘corporate culture’, Iveković highlighted the interdependence of so-called ‘immaterial’ and ‘material’ workers, foregrounding ongoing modes of taking the latter for granted. Keti Chukhrov observes that the ‘class gap within the “class” of immaterial workers is enormous’ as ‘the bulk of immaterial labour workers make no use whatsoever of their higher education and are working outside their specialization’. Moreover, she argues compellingly against the contemporary art-world myth that ‘“revolutionary” vocabulary and “proletarian” poetics are predominantly employed in the discourse of contemporary criticism and the creative industries, and rarely emerge in the realm of unprestigious material labour’. In view of these and other problematic assumptions, she notes that

zh: 有趣的是，西方艺术家调查日常化、低薪的工业劳动的作品，总是显眼地带有一种不可能性的印记：不可能有一个由泛欧洲中产阶级——包括物质劳动工作者和不受尊崇职业的代表——所建构的共享文化空间。
en: it is interesting that the work of Western artists investigating the  routine industrial, poorly paid labour is always conspicuously  marked by the impossibility of a shared cultural space constructed  by a pan-European middle class that includes material labour  workers and representatives of non-prestigious professions.

zh: 她接着说：
en: She continues:

zh: 在发达国家的社会空间中，体力劳动是不可见的；而一旦进入视野，它就被看作某种徘徊于猎奇与淫秽之间的东西。……物质劳动见证了日常化、机械性劳动与中产阶级生活及活动的智性—创造性文化空间之间致命的分裂。
en: In the social space of developed countries, physical labour is  invisible; and if it comes into view, it is seen as something hovering  between the exotic and the obscene. … Material labour testifies  to the fatal division between routine, mechanical labour, and the  intellectual-creative and cultural space of middle-class life and  activity.

zh: 丘赫罗夫主张，有必要继续保有一种对非剥削与非商品化之可能性的感觉，即“一般性的潜能，而不在物质劳动与非物质劳动之间实行隔离——不从人类学意义上把人划分为两个生产者种族”。
en: Chukhrov argues for the need to continue to retain a sense of the possibility of non-exploitation and non-commodification, of the ‘potential of the general without a segregation between material and immaterial labour – without an anthropological division of people into two races of producers’.

zh: 伊韦科维奇试图在影片最后一幕克服这种分裂，以她与纪录片拍摄对象作为后社会主义女性的共同经验为基础，与她们搭建一座共同的桥。清洁女工结束一天工作后，镜头显示一扇沉重的钢门轻轻关闭，也许是在指涉电影史上工厂大门打开、工人涌出的标志性时刻。然后，出人意料地，一只八音盒响起。它奏出《国际歌》单薄发脆的版本，镜头跟随一位高个年轻金发女人忧郁地沿着后勤走廊行走，一边走一边给八音盒上发条；她缓缓走在走廊里。

摄影机转向一位年长女性面部的特写。她戴着珍珠耳环，眼神遥远。她的神情表明她记得太清楚了。房间里聚集着各个年龄的其他女性的面孔，她们与艺术家一起听着这曲调，轮流被镜头审视，有些一起出现，有些单独出现。每个人都极其严肃，没人在笑。她们显然明白这里所表达的意思。几乎所有人都来自前社会主义国家，和艺术家本人一样。有些人开始跟着点头，另一些人看上去难过，甚至快要落泪，坚强外表濒临崩溃。她们的集体处境显然充满反讽；她们正生活在梦想的失败之中。画面变黑。八音盒音乐越来越慢。镜头摇回空荡的走廊，其红色管道开始可疑地像是社会主义过去之承诺的非自愿纪念碑。突然，红色似乎无处不在：其中一层整个被漆成红色。然而，在地面之上，镜头回到浮华的新自由主义当下。尽管银行总部位于维也纳，所有标识却都用英语；浮夸地命名为“宏伟大厅”（Grand Hall）的空间开始坐满人。城市交响曲，或至少其园区微观世界，正在重新开始。清洁已完成，白领员工陆续到来接手，而不可见的清洁工该消失回她们不可见的生活了。园区接下来的一部分日程与她们无关。正如网站介绍“埃斯特集团作为雇主”之优点的部分所宣称：“赚钱可以具有更深的含义”——尽管严格来说，清洁工并非埃斯特集团的雇员。
en: Iveković attempts to overcome such a division in the final scene of her film, building a common bridge with the subjects of her documentary, on the platform of their shared experience as post-socialist women. After the cleaners have finished their working day, the camera shows a heavy steel door gently closing, perhaps in reference to the iconic cinematic moment of the factory doors opening and the workers flooding out. Then, unexpectedly, a music box starts up. It plays a tinny version of ‘The Internationale’ and the camera tracks a tall young blonde woman melancholically walking down a service corridor winding it up as she goes, as she walks slowly down a corridor.

The camera shifts to a close-up of an older woman’s face. She wears pearl earrings and a far-away look in her eye. Her look suggests that she remembers all too well. Other women’s faces, of all ages, gathered in the room, together with the artist, listening to the tune together, are scrutinized, in turn, some together, some along. Everyone looks deadly serious and no one is laughing. They clearly get the point being made here. Almost all are from former socialist countries, like the artist herself. Some begin to nod along, others looks upset, even on the verge of tears, their tough exteriors threatening to crumble. There is clearly an irony in their collective situation; they are living the failure of the dream. The screen goes black. The music box music gets slower and slower. The camera pans back to the empty corridor, its red pipes beginning to look suspiciously like involuntary monuments to the promise of the socialist past. Suddenly red seems to be everywhere: one of the floors is painted red in its entirety. Above ground, though, the camera returns to the flashy neoliberal present. All the signage is in English, despite the bank’s headquarters being in Vienna, and the pompously named ‘Grand Hall’ is beginning to fill up. The city symphony, or at least its campus microcosm, is starting over. The cleaning is done, the white collar staff are arriving to take over, and it is time for the invisible cleaners to disappear back to their invisible lives. The next part of the day on campus is not about them. As the section of the website introducing the merits of ‘Erste Group as an Employer’ proclaims: ‘Earning money can have a deeper meaning’ – though, technically, the cleaners are not Erste group employees.
